traveler: Hiram Abiff (Hiram of Tyre, Huram-abi, the widow's son)
title: The Widow's Son: Two Verses of Bronze, and the Grave Dug for Him in London
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Tyre, the widow's son is born
stops.date_confidence: no birth year survives in any source; the date is a placeholder set roughly a generation before Solomon's fourth year
stops.campa: In the island city of Tyre a son is born to a widow and to a father who works in brass. First Kings names him simply Hiram. Second Chronicles calls him Huram-abi, Huram his father, a term of honor from a king to a master workman that later readers in London will take for a surname. No year is given, no house, no street. The city is the only fixed point the texts allow, a harbor of dyers and metal-founders on a rock offshore, and the trade he will be famous for is his father's trade before it is his.
stops.quote: And king Solomon sent and fetched Hiram out of Tyre. He was a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in brass: and he was filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass. And he came to king Solomon, and wrought all his work.
suggested_refs: The excavated Phoenician harbour and island quarter of Tyre (Sour), Lebanon

stops.name: Zorah, the mother the Chronicler gives him
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the text gives a tribe and no place, and this pin stands for the tribe
stops.campa: Second Chronicles gives the craftsman's mother as a woman of the daughters of Dan. Zorah stands for that claim, a hill town in the western foothills where Judges places Manoah of the family of the Danites. It is nowhere near Naphtali. A second claim locates her in Galilee instead: the two books disagree about the woman who bore him, and neither offers a way to choose between them. What survives of his mother is a tribe, asserted twice, differently, and a widowhood asserted once.
suggested_refs: The tell of Zorah (Tzor'a) above the Sorek valley

stops.name: Hazor, the mother the Book of Kings gives him
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no verse ties the family to this town or to any town in Naphtali
stops.campa: First Kings puts the widow in the tribe of Naphtali, in upper Galilee, a hundred miles north of the Danite foothills. Hazor marks the territory and nothing narrower. The men who later build a mystery on this craftsman never trouble with the discrepancy. He is a widow's son. That phrase, and not the tribe, is what the lodges keep, repeated in the dark by candidates who have been told they are standing at a grave. Nothing in the ritual requires the woman to have come from anywhere.
suggested_refs: Tel Hazor, the largest tell in upper Galilee, standing for the tribal territory

segments.name: The Summons and the Road South

stops.name: Tyre, the league between the two kings
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Hiram king of Tyre, who ever loved David, cuts a league with David's son: cedar and cypress for wheat and pressed oil. Solomon's journey holds this pin at this year. Into the bargain the king puts a man, another Hiram, cunning in brass. Two Hirams stand in the same sentence, the monarch and the founder, and three thousand years of tradition will confuse them and then separate them again. The letter Chronicles preserves is the king's, and it is the king who calls the craftsman a cunning man endued with understanding.
stops.quote: And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding, of Huram my father's, the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him.
suggested_refs: The harbour of Tyre, from which the league and the craftsman both go south

stops.name: The cedars of Lebanon, the rafts bound for the sea
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no verse places the craftsman on this mountain, and the pin belongs to the timber
stops.campa: Thirty thousand men go up by courses to the mountain, and Hiram's servants hew the great cedars and bind them into floats for the sea. Solomon's journey holds this pin at this year. The craftsman is a founder and not a carpenter, and no text puts him on the slope. The stop is here because the same treaty moves both the wood and the man, and because the road south for anything Tyrian begins where the king's servants are already at work under the resin.
suggested_refs: The Cedars of God (Arz el-Rab) above Bsharri, Lebanon

stops.name: Joppa, the timber comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the port is attested for the timber, the craftsman's passage through it is inference
stops.campa: Cedar cut in Lebanon comes down to Joppa in floats and goes up to Jerusalem overland, by the arrangement Chronicles records between the two kings. No verse says the craftsman travels with the timber. The port is the fixed conduit for his raw material, and tradition brings the man through it as well. Masonic legend will reuse this harbor at the far end of the story, when three murderers try to take ship here and find they cannot leave the country without the king's pass.
suggested_refs: The old harbour of Jaffa, landfall of the Lebanese timber floats
sources: Masonic third-degree ritual tradition, for the later reuse of the port

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: Solomon sends and fetches him
stops.date_confidence: traditional; 1 Kings 6:1 dates the start of building to the month of Ziv in Solomon's fourth year
stops.campa: Solomon sends and fetches Hiram out of Tyre, and he comes and works all his work. The text calls him filled with wisdom, and understanding, and cunning to work all works in brass. He arrives in the fourth year of the reign, in the month of Ziv, with the foundation being laid. Solomon's journey holds this pin through the whole building, and Nebuchadnezzar's journey holds it again four centuries later, at the end of it. Everything the lodges eventually stage on this rock rests on two verses of a chapter about metalwork.
suggested_refs: The Temple Mount platform, the atlas pin shared by Solomon, Sheba, and Nebuchadnezzar

stops.name: Jerusalem, the queen of the south while the bronze is still to be cast
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the atlas holds Sheba at Jerusalem in this year
stops.campa: The queen of Sheba comes up with camels bearing spices and gold and precious stones, and sees the house, and the meat of the table, and the ascent by which the king goes up. Her journey holds this pin at this year. She is told that the half was not told her. The craftsman is not named in her audience, and no source puts the two of them in a room. The marvels she is shown are in part his work, and a French opera will one day hand her to him as a lover and kill him for it.
suggested_refs: The Jerusalem pin held in common by sheba.journey.json and this route

stops.name: The plain of Jordan near Succoth, the clay that will hold a mould
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Succoth is commonly identified with Tell Deir Alla, a convention rather than a certainty
stops.campa: The king casts the vessels in the plain of Jordan, in the thick clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan, because nothing nearer Jerusalem will hold a mould at this scale. This is the only place in the craftsman's whole biblical record fixed to a named ground rather than to a city. He works forty miles from the building, down in a river valley, and the finished bronze goes up to the mountain by road. The reason the text gives is the ground itself: clay thick enough to take the pour.
suggested_refs: Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, the usual identification of Succoth
sources: standard biblical archaeology on Succoth, identification not textually certain

stops.name: Zarethan, the other boundary of the casting ground
stops.date_confidence: the site is contested; this pin follows the Tell el-Mazar identification on the west bank, against Nelson Glueck's older east-bank Tell es-Sa'idiyeh
stops.campa: Zarethan names the far edge of the clay flats, and nobody is sure where it is. Glueck proposed Tell es-Sa'idiyeh on the east bank; the reading now preferred puts it at Tell el-Mazar on the west, in Wadi Far'a. The verse gives two names for one stretch of riverbank, and only one of them is even provisionally located. This record takes the western reading and keeps the older one on the page rather than dropping it quietly. The ground that shaped the pillars cannot be pointed at.
suggested_refs: Tell el-Mazar and Tell es-Sa'idiyeh, the two competing Zarethans

stops.name: The porch of the Temple, Jachin and Boaz set up
stops.date_confidence: traditional; within the seven years of building given by 1 Kings 6:38
stops.campa: He casts two hollow pillars of brass, eighteen cubits high, crowned with lily-work and networks of pomegranates, and they are set before the porch of the house. Solomon names the right one Jachin and the left one Boaz. Every lodge room furnished since 1723 puts two pillars at its door on the strength of this passage. In First Kings the pillars are not symbols. They are castings, measured in cubits, a line of twelve cubits to compass them and four fingers of metal in the wall.
stops.quote: And he set up the right pillar, and called the name thereof Jachin: and he set up the left pillar, and called the name thereof Boaz.
suggested_refs: Reconstruction drawings of Jachin and Boaz from the measurements in 1 Kings 7:15-22

stops.name: The court of the Temple, the molten sea on twelve oxen
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: He casts the great sea, round, ten cubits from brim to brim and five in height, standing on twelve oxen, three looking north, three west, three south, three east, their hinder parts inward. It holds two thousand baths and is set on the right side of the house eastward, over against the south. Nothing else credited to him is on this scale. The ritual that later kills him never mentions it: the lodges keep the two pillars and forget the sea, which was the harder casting.
suggested_refs: The molten sea and its twelve oxen, reconstructed from 1 Kings 7:23-26

stops.name: Jerusalem, the vessels finished and the house dedicated without him
stops.date_confidence: traditional; 1 Kings 6:38 dates completion to the month of Bul in the eleventh year, conventionally 959 or 958 BC
stops.campa: The pots, the shovels, the basins, the fleshhooks, all of bright brass, and the account closes with the phrase that becomes his name. Then the house is finished, the ark brought up, the cloud fills the holy place, and sacrifices are offered past counting. Hiram of Tyre is not at the dedication and is not mentioned in it. The text that made him has nothing further to say once the metal is set in place. There is no farewell, no payment recorded, no return to Tyre, and no death.
stops.quote: And Huram made the pots, and the shovels, and the basons. And Huram finished the work that he was to make for king Solomon for the house of God... The pots also, and the shovels, and the fleshhooks, and all their instruments, did Huram his father make to king Solomon for the house of the LORD of bright brass.
suggested_refs: 1 Kings 8, the dedication narrative in which the craftsman does not appear

segments.name: The Murder That Is Not in the Book

stops.name: The unfinished sanctuary, high twelve at noon
stops.date_confidence: legendary; no source outside Masonic ritual records any of this, and the ritual supplies no date. The nine stops that follow are one legendary day
stops.campa: The legend holds that the master enters the unfinished sanctuary each day at high twelve, when the craftsmen have gone to refreshment, to offer his devotions and draw his designs on the trestle-board. No biblical verse describes the habit. It enters print in 1730, in a hostile pamphlet written by a man exposing the lodges, and passes from there into ritual as fact. The custom exists to put him alone in a building, at a known hour, near a door: everything the murder requires.
stops.quote: In the Building of Solomon's Temple he was Master-Mason, and at high 12 at Noon, when the Men was gone to refresh themselves, as was his usual Custom, he came to survey the Works.
stops.quote_source: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (London, 1730, 3rd ed.), catechism text
suggested_refs: The trestle-board of the Master Mason degree, on which the designs are drawn
sources: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (1730), Internet Archive djvu transcript

stops.name: The south gate, the first blow
stops.date_confidence: legendary; one hour of one day that no source outside the lodge records
stops.campa: Fifteen fellowcrafts conspire to force the master's word from him. Twelve repent. Three keep to the plan and take the three gates. At the south gate the first demands the word, is refused, and strikes him across the throat with a twenty-four-inch gauge. American workings name this man Jubela. English Emulation ritual leaves all three unnamed, and the names Jubela, Jubelo, and Jubelum belong to the Preston-Webb monitorial line rather than to any English lodge. He staggers west, wounded, still holding what he has.
suggested_refs: The twenty-four-inch gauge, first of the three working tools turned into weapons
sources: Standard Masonic third-degree ritual, American (Preston-Webb) working
Emulation ritual, which leaves the three unnamed

stops.name: The west gate, the second blow
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the gate scheme itself is absent from the earliest printed version of 1730
stops.campa: At the west gate the second ruffian repeats the demand and strikes him across the breast with a square. The ritual gives every blow a named tool: gauge, square, setting maul, the working instruments of the craft turned against the craft's master. Nothing outside the lodge confirms a single detail, and Prichard's printed version of 1730 has no three gates and no names at all. The apparatus grows across the eighteenth century, one exposure at a time, until it looks like something remembered.
stops.quote: By Three Great Knocks, or the Death of our Master Hiram.
stops.quote_source: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (London, 1730, 3rd ed.), answer to how Master Masons are made
suggested_refs: The square, second of the three tools, in the Master Mason tracing boards
sources: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (1730), for the absence of the gates

stops.name: The east gate, the setting maul
stops.date_confidence: legendary
stops.campa: At the gate facing the sunrise the third man demands the word a last time. The master answers that it is held by three, Solomon, Hiram king of Tyre, and himself, and that no one of them can give it alone; then he is killed with a setting maul. That refusal is the hinge of the whole degree. Because the word is held jointly, his death does not withhold it, it loses it. Accounts that make him sole possessor of the word break the logic of the story they are telling.
suggested_refs: The setting maul, the third tool and the killing blow, at the gate of the rising sun
sources: contradiction flagged against sources that make him sole holder of the word

stops.name: A low hill west of Moriah, the rubbish and the acacia
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the ritual gives a direction and no location, and this pin is notional
stops.campa: They carry the body out and hide it under rubbish until high twelve again, then take it by night to a low hill west of the Temple and bury it, planting a sprig of acacia at the head to find the place again. The hill is unnamed and unidentified. The pin here is a notional point inside the walled city and must not be read as a located grave: the ritual gives a compass direction and nothing else, and this record will not manufacture the rest. The acacia is the only marker, and it is planted by the murderers.
stops.quote: Carried him out at the West Door of the Temple, and hid him under some Rubbish till High 12 again.
stops.quote_source: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (London, 1730, 3rd ed.), catechism text
suggested_refs: The sprig of acacia, the grave-marker that becomes the degree's emblem of immortality

stops.name: The hills above Joppa, the cave and the well
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the cave has no locatable site and this pin is the port of Joppa, not the cave
stops.campa: The three run for the coast, meaning to take ship at Joppa, and lie up by day in a cave above the port. Some tellings name the place Bendaco or Bendacca; the toponym is attested nowhere else and cannot be fixed. A searcher resting by a well hears one of them cry out that he would rather have had his throat cut than betray the secret, and that is how they are found. The pin is the harbor, which exists. The cave and the well are given no coordinates here because they have none.
suggested_refs: Variant place-names for the ruffians' cave, collected in Mackey's Encyclopedia
sources: Albert G. Mackey, Encyclopedia of Freemasonry (1873), for the variant names

stops.name: Jerusalem, the twelve who search and the sentence
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the workings disagree with each other about the place of execution
stops.campa: Solomon sends out the twelve who recanted, in parties of three, east and west and north and south. They find the acacia, and the grave, and then the men. Brought before the king the three confess and are executed, in some workings on the spot where the body lay, in others at the king's order in the city. The rituals do not agree and this record does not choose between them. The number fifteen belongs to the conspiracy, not to the search party, and sources that send out fifteen have miscounted.
suggested_refs: The four search parties of three, sent to the four points of the compass
sources: execution site varies between workings, contradiction unresolved

stops.name: The grave reopened, the raising near the Sanctum Sanctorum
stops.date_confidence: legendary; the ritual specifies fourteen days between the burial and the raising
stops.campa: After fourteen days the body is raised out of the rubbish and buried again as near the sanctuary as the law will permit. The lifting of it, by a grip that American workings call the lion's paw, becomes the central gesture of the third degree: the candidate is the corpse, and is raised. The ritual concedes the state the body is in by then. The words spoken over the grave are the ones a mason in distress is taught to use in the night, when the sign cannot be seen.
stops.quote: O Lord my God! is there no help for the widow's son?
stops.quote_source: Malcolm C. Duncan, Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor (New York: Dick & Fitzgerald, c. 1866), Master Mason degree
suggested_refs: The Grand Hailing Sign of Distress and the words attached to it in Duncan's Monitor
sources: Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor, Internet Archive full text

stops.name: The Temple, the substitute word
stops.date_confidence: legendary
stops.campa: The word died with him, so Solomon and the assembled masters agree on a substitute, to serve until some future age recovers the true one. The degree exists to install that arrangement: a word everyone agrees to use because the real one is gone, and a recovery always promised to a later age. No book of the Hebrew Bible records a death, a grave, a search, or a word. The murder, the ruffians, the acacia, and the substitute are absent from every source older than the 1720s.
suggested_refs: The substitute word of the Master Mason degree, held until the true word is recovered
sources: comparative absence across 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, and Josephus

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount: the bronze carried off
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the Babylonian Chronicle and 2 Kings; the day is the atlas convention
stops.campa: Nebuchadnezzar's men break up the pillars Jachin and Boaz, and the sea, and the bases, and carry the brass of them to Babylon; the pots and shovels go too. His journey holds this pin at this date. Everything the craftsman made is destroyed as metal, weighed and taken away for its value. No fragment survives, no mould, no inscription, no tool. The physical record of Hiram of Tyre ends here, four centuries after the casting, in an inventory of scrap.
suggested_refs: 2 Kings 25:13-17, the breaking up of the bronze

stops.name: Qabr Hiram near Hanaouay, the tomb of the wrong man
stops.date_confidence: the monument is dated by architectural parallel to the Persian period, four to six centuries after any Solomonic Hiram
stops.campa: Six kilometres southeast of Tyre, on the road to Qana, a great stone sarcophagus stands on a stepped plinth and is called Hiram's Tomb. Nineteenth-century travelers and Masonic pilgrims came out to see the grave of the Temple's builder. Its parallels are the tomb of Cyrus and the Gur-e-Dokhtar, which places it in the Persian period. If it honors any Hiram it honors the king, who died about 947 and was succeeded by his son Baal-Eser. It is the only grave the tradition can point at, and it is the wrong grave.
suggested_refs: The Qabr Hiram sarcophagus and plinth near Hanaouay, Lebanon
sources: Josephus on Hiram I's death, via Wikipedia 'Hiram I'

stops.name: Rome, Josephus writes and says nothing of a murder
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Antiquities of the Jews is conventionally dated to 93 or 94 AD
stops.campa: In Rome, Flavius Josephus finishes the Antiquities, drawing on the lost history of Menander of Ephesus for the Tyrian court records: Hiram's reign, his building works, his correspondence with Solomon, the archives at Tyre where the letters were said to be kept. He mentions no murdered master-builder. The first-century writer with the best access to Phoenician material has no Hiram Abiff at all, and that silence, held for another sixteen centuries, is the strongest dating evidence the record contains.
suggested_refs: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book VIII, on the Tyrian archives
sources: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews (1st century AD), via Wikipedia 'Hiram I'

stops.name: The Temple Mount, the Poor Knights take the platform
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the order's foundation is conventionally dated 1119 or 1120
stops.campa: Knights are given quarters on the platform above the ruins and take from it the name Poor Knights of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon. Jacques de Molay's journey carries that title to his election, and carries it to the fire in Paris in 1314. Some Masonic writers hold that the order brought the Hiramic legend out of the Holy Land into Europe. Mainstream historians of Freemasonry find no document connecting Templars to any eighteenth-century lodge. The claim is popular and the evidence for it is absent.
suggested_refs: The Al-Aqsa platform, Templar headquarters over the supposed site of the Temple
sources: disputed Templar-transmission theory, rejected by mainstream Masonic historiography

stops.name: Kilwinning, the lodge that claims descent from the builders
stops.date_confidence: attested from the Second Schaw Statutes of 1599; the claimed medieval antiquity is undocumented
stops.campa: The operative masons of Kilwinning claim a lineage running back to the men who raised the abbey on this ground, and beyond them to the guild mythology that eventually swallows Solomon's Temple whole. The lodge is documented from the Second Schaw Statutes of 1599. When it petitioned in 1736 it could not prove its antiquity. No Kilwinning document ties its masons to any story about Hiram before the speculative era, and the claim of unbroken descent is the lodge's own tradition, not an external record.
suggested_refs: Kilwinning Abbey and the Mother Lodge, and the Second Schaw Statutes of 1599
sources: Kilwinning lodge tradition, unverified by independent record

stops.name: The Goose and Gridiron, the Grand Lodge founded
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four London lodges meet at an alehouse in St Paul's Churchyard on St John's day, constitute a Grand Lodge, and elect Anthony Sayer their Grand Master. Nothing about Hiram happens at this table. What is built here is a central authority with a standard working, and within six years it prints a history of itself. A story told in one room can now be told the same way in a thousand rooms. The legend needs that machinery, and until this morning the machinery does not exist.
suggested_refs: The site of the Goose and Gridiron alehouse, St Paul's Churchyard, London

stops.name: London, Anderson's Constitutions and the name Abif
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: James Anderson compiles the Constitutions of the Free-Masons to the order of Desaguliers and by approval of a Grand Lodge committee. In it he settles a Hebrew ambiguity by force: Huram abiv, Huram his father, becomes Hiram Abif, a man with a surname. Reformation translators had left the reading open and Anderson closes it. He also organizes the Temple workforce into Masonic ranks and presents the arrangement as history rather than allegory. The 1738 edition rewrites the wording; the name is fixed here.
stops.quote: ...that Hiram, King of Tyre, sent to King Solomon his namesake Hiram Abif, the Prince of Architects.
stops.quote_source: James Anderson, The Constitutions of the Free-Masons (London, 1723), verified in the Internet Archive scan constitutionsoff00anderich
suggested_refs: The frontispiece and title page of Anderson's Constitutions, London, 1723
sources: James Anderson, Constitutions of the Free-Masons (1723), Internet Archive full text

stops.name: London, the third degree and the man who probably wrote it
stops.date_confidence: the separation of the third degree is dated by consensus to the mid-1720s; the exact year is disputed
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years the Master Mason degree separates from the two craft degrees and acquires a corpse. Christopher Powell argued in 2021 that John Theophilus Desaguliers, Royal Society experimenter and Grand Lodge officer, most likely wrote the Hiramic legend and put it into the degree. Paul Naudon traced its shape to the death of Renaud de Montauban, killed with a hammer while working as a mason at Cologne, his body hidden and afterward found. No contemporary document names an author.
suggested_refs: The chanson de geste of the Four Sons of Aymon, and the death of Renaud at Cologne
sources: Christopher Powell (2021), cited via Wikipedia 'Hiram Abiff'
Paul Naudon (2005), cited via Wikipedia 'Hiram Abiff'

stops.name: Edinburgh, the Graham Manuscript
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1726; the link to the Hiramic legend is scholarly inference, not stated in the manuscript
stops.campa: A Scottish manuscript tells of the sons of Noah going to their father's grave in hope of finding something of him, and raising the body by grip and by word. Many Masonic historians read the passage as the Hiramic legend's ancestor. It names Noah and not Hiram, and the manuscript makes no such equation itself: the lineage is an inference drawn by later readers. It is nonetheless the closest thing to a pre-1730 witness that the surviving record supplies.
suggested_refs: The Graham Manuscript of 1726 and its raising of the body of Noah
sources: interpretive link to the Hiramic legend is scholarly inference

stops.name: London, Masonry Dissected
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Samuel Prichard, an outsider and probably an enemy of the Craft, prints the catechism of the three degrees for anyone with a shilling. In it the master workman is killed, hidden under rubbish, and found by fifteen brothers sent out by the king. There are no gates yet, and no names for the killers, and the Latin the catechism quotes is garbled and left uncorrected. It is hostile, incomplete, and the earliest substantial printed trace of the story the lodges are by then already telling.
stops.quote: Fifteen Loving Brothers, by Order of King Solomon, went out of the West Door of the Temple... found him decently buried in a handsome Grave.
stops.quote_source: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (London, 1730, 3rd ed.), catechism text
suggested_refs: The 1730 title page of Masonry Dissected and its catechism of the three degrees
sources: Samuel Prichard, Masonry Dissected (1730), Internet Archive djvu transcript

stops.name: Paris, Ramsay's oration
stops.date_confidence: delivered at Paris in 1736; the revised written discourse is of March 1737 and its delivery is not confirmed
stops.campa: Andrew Michael Ramsay tells a Paris audience that Freemasonry descends from crusading knights, meaning the Hospitallers, though his listeners hear Templars. He sends the revised text to Cardinal Fleury the following March and is answered with an interdiction of Masonic assemblies. He narrates no murder. He supplies the frame on which the continental higher degrees are built, and those degrees pile Solomonic furniture on the third degree's grave. Giulio Camillo's journey holds this Paris pin two centuries earlier.
suggested_refs: Ramsay's Discourse, sent to Cardinal Fleury on 20 March 1737

stops.name: London, the second Constitutions
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Anderson revises his book. Hiram Abif is now the most accomplish'd Designer and Operator upon Earth, and his death is referred to in a Grand Lodge publication. It is often said that 1738 marks the first appearance of the name in an authorized book. That is false, and this record marks it false: the 1723 edition was authorized too and already carried it. The claim survives because the second edition is the one later masons owned, and the first is the one they quoted from memory.
suggested_refs: James Anderson, The New Book of Constitutions, London, 1738
sources: James Anderson, The New Book of Constitutions (1738), Internet Archive full text
contradiction flagged against the claim of first official use in 1738

stops.name: London, Preston's Illustrations of Masonry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: William Preston publishes a history and a lecture system, twelve lectures to each degree, delivered for a fee at the Mitre Tavern from 1774. He does not print ritual and does not dramatize the murder. Preston is repeatedly credited with the three gates, the named ruffians, the acacia sprig, and the lion's paw, and he supplied none of them. What he supplied was the moral and educational apparatus that made the legend teachable in a lodge room, and every English working since has been taught through it.
suggested_refs: Preston's twelve lectures per degree, given at the Mitre Tavern from 1774

stops.name: Roslin, the apprentice and the pillar
stops.date_confidence: the local legend is dated only to the eighteenth century; the chapel was founded in 1446
stops.campa: A Scottish story attaches itself to a carved pillar in a fifteenth-century chapel: a master mason kills his apprentice in jealousy, the boy having finished the work while the master was away. It is a craftsman murdered over skill, and it is not the Hiramic legend and has no Masonic origin. Robert L. D. Cooper dates the third degree to about 1720, three centuries after the chapel's founding, and attributes the Rosslyn connection to speculative writing that began in the 1980s.
suggested_refs: The Apprentice Pillar in Rosslyn Chapel, Roslin, Midlothian
sources: Robert L. D. Cooper, cited in Wikipedia 'Rosslyn Chapel'

stops.name: Albany, New York, Webb's Freemason's Monitor
stops.date_confidence: attested by the copyright date of 14 September 1797
stops.campa: Thomas Smith Webb copyrights the Freemason's Monitor on the fourteenth of September and gives American lodges the wording they still use. Preston's lecture system is adapted, the drama around it is fixed, and the lion's paw and the names Jubela, Jubelo, and Jubelum become standard on this side of the ocean while English Emulation leaves the three men nameless. The difference between the English Hiram and the American one begins at this printing and has never closed.
suggested_refs: The Freemason's Monitor, or Illustrations of Masonry, Albany, 1797
sources: Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor (1797)

stops.name: Charleston, the Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1801; the sources consulted here do not fix the day
stops.campa: The Scottish Rite's Southern Jurisdiction constitutes itself at Charleston, and the higher degrees acquire an institution. Hiram's death belongs to the third degree and not to the thirty-two above it, but the temple furniture those degrees elaborate rests on his grave, and their nineteenth-century rewriting will be done in this city. A parallel Scottish Rite body will later be seated at Cadiz, carrying the same American degree structure back across the Atlantic to the continent Freemasonry first crossed from.
suggested_refs: The Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction, founded at Charleston in 1801
sources: Scottish Rite Supreme Council founding record, Charleston, 1801

stops.name: Paris, Nerval renames him Adoniram
stops.date_confidence: attested to the publication of the Voyage en Orient in 1851
stops.campa: Gerard de Nerval prints in the Voyage en Orient the most elaborate literary retelling the legend has, framed as a tale told across two weeks in an eastern coffeehouse. He calls the master Adoniram and gives him Balkis, Queen of the Morning, against Soliman, Prince of the Genii. He is reported to have worked real Masonic passwords into the text. The story leaves the lodge room at this address and enters ordinary nineteenth-century reading, where it stops being a secret and becomes a plot.
suggested_refs: Gerard de Nerval, Voyage en Orient, 1851, the Histoire de la reine du matin
sources: Gerard de Nerval, Voyage en Orient (1851), cited via Wikipedia 'Hiram Abiff'

stops.name: Paris, Salle Le Peletier: La Reine de Saba
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Gounod sets Nerval, to a libretto by Paul Barbier and Michel Carre. Adoniram casts the sea of bronze on stage, Balkis loves him and not the king, and three treacherous workmen kill him. Barbier's journey holds this pin at this date and states the matter without hedging: it is the Hiram legend, the very heart of the Masonic myth. The queen who came up to Jerusalem in the tenth century before Christ and the craftsman who never met her are married off in a Paris opera house.
suggested_refs: The Salle Le Peletier and the score of Gounod's La Reine de Saba, 1862

stops.name: New York, Duncan's Ritual and Monitor
stops.date_confidence: Dick and Fitzgerald, New York, dated c. 1866; the edition year is approximate
stops.campa: Malcolm Duncan prints the American degrees with diagrams, and the third degree is there entire: the grave, the raising, the grip, and the words to be used in the night or the dark when the sign cannot be seen. What began in 1730 as a hostile exposure has become a manual bought by masons themselves. The cry Duncan records at the graveside is the one line of the whole tradition that escaped the lodges completely, and it turns up now wherever the phrase widow's son is spoken.
suggested_refs: The Master Mason degree diagrams in Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor
sources: Malcolm C. Duncan, Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor, Internet Archive full text

stops.name: Charleston, Pike's Morals and Dogma
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Albert Pike rewrites the Scottish Rite and publishes Morals and Dogma, reading Hiram into solar myth and the mystery religions: a god who dies and is raised, dressed here as a bronze-founder. Pike does not offer the reading as history and it is not history. It is the point at which the murdered craftsman is absorbed into comparative religion, and the point from which a century of occult writing takes him, Theodor Reuss and Rene Guenon among the readers downstream.
suggested_refs: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, 1871

stops.name: Washington, Mackey's Encyclopedia
stops.date_confidence: 1873 per Wikipedia; the date 1874 is often given and 1874 imprints exist
stops.campa: Albert Mackey, who worked from Charleston until 1870 and from Washington afterward, publishes the Encyclopedia of Freemasonry. He treats Hiram Abiff as a symbol of the initiate's own death and rebirth rather than as a man who lived. He records the variant names, gates, and burial details across the workings instead of smoothing them into one account. The reference books that follow him mostly do smooth them, and the disagreements he preserved are the ones this record has been able to see.
suggested_refs: Albert G. Mackey, Encyclopedia of Freemasonry, first edition
sources: Albert G. Mackey, Encyclopedia of Freemasonry (1873)

stops.name: Chester, a Hiram at St John's
stops.date_confidence: the source gives a year and no medium; treat as a thin record
stops.campa: A depiction of Hiram as architect, dated 1900, is recorded at the church of St John the Baptist in Chester. What it is made of, where in the building it stands, and who made it are not stated by the source, and the church's own published inventory of its Victorian work does not mention it at all. The pin is set on the church rather than on any object inside it, because no object has been located and none is described. Somewhere in an English parish church a Tyrian founder is shown holding a plan.
suggested_refs: St John the Baptist's church, Chester, and its unlisted Hiram of 1900
sources: Wikipedia, 'St John the Baptist's Church, Chester', which does not mention it

stops.name: Berlin, Kruch's bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2013
stops.campa: A bronze statue of Hiram Abiff by Nickolaus-Otto Kruch is set up in Berlin. The man the statue commemorates never existed as its subject; the man in First Kings worked metal and is commemorated nowhere. Theodor Reuss's journey holds this pin, in a Berlin of Masonic and occult orders working the same three-ruffians material a century before. Three thousand years after the plain of Jordan, a founder casts a founder in brass, and the man in the mould is a legend written in London in the 1720s.
suggested_refs: Nickolaus-Otto Kruch's bronze of Hiram Abiff, Berlin, 2013
